source.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) transfer across base and finetuned language models?

page_placements.theme: Correspondence of SAE features across models, finetunes, domains and pruning

record.tranche_reason: The post measures whether base-model SAEs transfer to fine-tuned models, not whether increasing dictionary size splits coarse features into finer features.
record.gate_note: No dictionary-size sweep or measurement of coarse-to-fine feature partitions is reported. The rows below record related SAE transferability results, but none tests the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The post applies fixed-size base-model SAEs (16384 and 65536 features) to finetuned models and measures reconstruction metrics and feature activation and logit similarity. There is no dictionary-size sweep, no coarse-to-fine feature analysis, no absorption or hierarchy measurement, and no comparison of training objectives. Feature splitting is not named; Towards Monosemanticity is cited only for its universality metrics. None of V1–V6 is tested. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses', since splitting is never discussed.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that transferability 'depends' on the model and finetune: Gemma-2b transfers poorly and Mistral-7B well. Weight-deviation or activation-similarity metrics may predict this in advance. Some Gemma features may still transfer despite failed reconstruction, though the authors question how significant this is.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares base-model SAEs on base and finetuned models; it does not test the dictionary-size splitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results differ substantially between the Gemma-2b Python-code finetune and the Mistral-7B MetaMath finetune.

fits_no_version.finding: Base-model SAE reconstruction collapsed on the Gemma-2b Python-code finetune (R2 0.97 to -10.27) but held up on Mistral-7B MetaMath (R2 0.68 to 0.58).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE transferability from base to finetuned models is model- and finetuning-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Regular-feature activation similarity was 0.39 for Gemma and 0.958 for Mistral; about 10% of Gemma features exceeded 0.8. Logit similarity was high in both (0.952, 0.9996), which the authors attribute largely to an unchanged unembedding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some SAE features may transfer to a finetuned model even when overall reconstruction fails.

fits_no_version.finding: Global mean cosine similarity of residual activations was 0.6691 (Gemma) and 0.9648 (Mistral), tracking the SAE transfer results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similarity of residual activations between base and finetuned models anecdotally predicts SAE transferability.

record.problems: The study covers only two model pairs and one residual layer per model, uses the base SAE training datasets, and does not conduct a feature interpretability or circuit analysis. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the listed measurements.
record.rows_left_out: Other SAE metrics, dead-feature activation errors, and feature-density results are not included because they concern base-to-finetuned transfer rather than the dictionary-size splitting claim.

untested.parts: All: no change in dictionary size, no coarse-to-fine replacement, coverage or direction proximity measured.
All: uses large-model open SAE releases (SAELens Gemma-2b, Mistral-7B), but not for splitting.
All: no feature families or hierarchy analysed.
All: no parent/child latent firing, and no size or sparsity variation.
All: no comparison of latents across SAE sizes.
All: no training-objective comparison and no Matryoshka SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none'] with cannot_determine states. Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only', because the post never addresses splitting, absorption or canonical units. It cites Towards Monosemanticity only for its universality metrics. This is a non-peer-reviewed Alignment Forum post.

versions.untested_parts: Dictionary-size growth, feature replacement, coverage of the same inputs, and proximity of split feature directions.
Splitting across large models or open SAE releases.
Nested feature families, their geometric closeness, and whether they mirror a concept hierarchy.
Parent-child firing overlap and effects of SAE size or sparsity on absorption.
Decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents and the presence of novel latents.
Whether the training objective causes splitting, and whether Matryoshka SAEs or other objectives change it.

relation.reason: The post never mentions feature splitting. It cites Towards Monosemanticity, the source of splitting, only for the SAE setup and the feature-universality method. Its own SAE-transfer measurements are not a discussion of the claim, so cites_only fits better than discusses.

tranche.reason: Studies SAE transfer across finetunes with fixed dictionary sizes (16384, 65536). No dictionary-size sweep, splitting, absorption or hierarchy test, and it does not use splitting as a tool.

source_check.notes: Both rows hold SAE-transfer R2 values, not feature-splitting results, so they have no version link and cannot_determine is right. The Gemma finetune is built on Gemma-2b Instruct. R2 is computed after outlier filtering (0.24% Gemma, 0.7% Mistral). The pack's 0/2 'numbers found' comes from table cells run together in the text. Both values are there.

statements.correction: Gemma-2b base SAE: R2 0.97 on base, -10.27 on Python-codes finetune (built on Instruct). Mistral-7B: 0.68 to 0.58 on MetaMath.
statements.problem: Numbers match the text. Minor: the Gemma Python-codes model is a finetune of Gemma-2b Instruct, not of the base directly.
